card.hook: Kagoshima has a neighbour that smokes all day, and it's just 4 km away across the water. Most people come to town for this one view, and you can fit the rooftops, the bay and the volcano into a single frame.
card.stand_here: Head up to the Shiroyama Park observation deck (城山公園展望台) at the top of the Shiroyama promenade. Face out over the city and Kagoshima Bay, and Sakurajima rises up behind the water. The climb is steep, so the city sightseeing bus is a good shortcut.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic city, bay and volcano shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the peaks closer and catch any ash plume. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground, because the volcano will look smaller.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, then tap the volcano and slide it a little darker so the sky and ash plume keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually clearest, with fewer people. The city lights after dark are a good second choice, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep them sharp. Ash and haze are common, so check the sky before you climb.
card.selfie_here: On the Shiroyama Park observation deck, stand on the right-hand side of the bench, which keeps the bushes on the left out of your shot. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the volcano and city over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't go near the volcano's craters, and one guide gives a 2 km no-entry zone. Yunohira Observation Deck is a safe, accessible place to watch it up close. The Shiroyama deck is described as a free viewpoint open all day, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fit rooftops, bay, volcano and a puff of ash into one frame, then see if you can look relaxed about it.
card.good_to_know: Sakurajima has three peaks, and the highest, Kita-dake, rises to 1,117 m. It has been erupting almost constantly since 1955, so a little ash is normal. It was once a true island, until the huge 1914 eruption sent lava into the strait and joined it to the mainland.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the Shiroyama Park observation deck (城山公園展望台) at the top of the Shiroyama promenade. Face out over the city and Kagoshima Bay, and Sakurajima rises up behind the water. The climb is steep, so the city sightseeing bus is a good shortcut.

card.hook: Here's a garden that got a volcano for free. The designers at Sengan-en used Sakurajima across Kagoshima Bay as 'borrowed scenery', so the mountain sits behind the ponds and paths like a giant painted backdrop.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m north of the subject, and face south. Take a few shots there, then wander towards the garden and try new spots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the garden and the bay together. Tap 0.5x in tighter spots to squeeze in a pond or path, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull Sakurajima closer or pick out a lantern or some bamboo.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the line of the bay on the upper third, and keep some water, a lantern or leaves low in the frame so the picture has depth.
card.best_time: Morning or later in the afternoon gives softer light on the garden and a gentler sky behind the volcano than midday. Late morning is also nice at the stone bridge. Avoid shooting straight into the light, because Sakurajima can turn into a dark silhouette.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the stone bridge in the garden with the pond and waterfall behind you, and use the front camera. For a second option, stand by the large stone lantern with the bamboo grove as your backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally welcome in the gardens, but flash may be restricted inside the residence and museum. There isn't much shade, so bring sunscreen and water on sunny days. It may be a ticketed garden with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a picture with something from the garden in front, the bay in the middle and the volcano at the top. Bonus points if you have to take three steps to the left to make it line up.
card.good_to_know: The residence was built by Shimazu Mitsuhisa in 1658. In 1736 Shimazu Yoshitaka added a winding water feature and moso bamboo that came from China by way of the Ryūkyū Kingdom. Edward VIII visited in 1922, and the garden is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the neighbouring Shōko Shūseikan.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m north of the subject, and face south. Take a few shots there, then wander towards the garden and try new spots.

card.hook: This little hill is only 107 m high, yet it's where the Satsuma rebellion came to its end in 1877. So you get a big view and a big slice of history in one stop.
card.stand_here: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, near 城山展望台 (Shiroyama Observation Deck), and face north. Take a shot of the hill that way, then turn around and see what view opens up.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the view. Switch to 0.5x when you want more sky and scenery in one frame, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single details in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: If the sky is bright and the land below looks dark, tap the distance on your screen and slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: A clear day gives you the longest view. Morning or late afternoon usually has softer light than midday, so check the weather before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the face-cutout board of Saigo Takamori in front of the Shiroyama Teahouse shop, next to the observatory area in Shiroyama Park. Use the front camera at 0.5x and pop your face in. Fair warning: the observation deck probably won't be behind you, so think of it as a fun souvenir shot.
card.ask_someone: At the upper viewing point, one traveler reported volunteers in volunteer shirts offering to take photos for free, so hand over your phone and stand with the view behind you (it may not always be available).
card.rules_and_safety: Some small dirt paths around the top of the park have no lighting, and one reviewer advises against exploring them because of the risk of falling. Check current local information before you go in case there are any access notices.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the view fills the frame, then a second one using a branch or railing at the edge to add depth. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The hill was originally called Tsuru ga mine (鶴ヶ峯). It's best known as the place where the Battle of Shiroyama was fought in 1877, the closing episode of the Satsuma rebellion. That's why many visitors come for the history as well as the view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, near 城山展望台 (Shiroyama Observation Deck), and face north. Take a shot of the hill that way, then turn around and see what view opens up.

card.hook: The whole building is shaped like a stingray and is around 150 m across, so no phone is going to fit all of it in. That's fine, because you're after the big, friendly sweep of it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 15 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east towards Kagoshima Aquarium. The building will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in as much of the long building as you can, then switch to 1x for a less stretched look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for details like the entrance or the signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't look tilted, and leave a little sky above it.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light. In the afternoon the sun will be behind you as you face east, so it should light up the side of the building you're looking at.
card.selfie_here: Try the Waterfront Park walkway next to the Dolphin Waterway, which runs beside the aquarium and the Sakurajima Ferry Terminal. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low, so the building is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the water on the same walkway, so they can fit the aquarium and the ferry terminal into one frame with you.
card.challenge: Take a shot with a perfectly level roofline and a nice strip of sky, then go up to the fifth floor and catch Sakurajima across the bay for your matching second picture.
card.good_to_know: Kagoshima Aquarium opened on 30 May 1997 and the route inside runs over five floors, from the basement up. The star residents are the whale sharks in the big Kuroshio tank, which holds 1,500,000 litres of water. The fifth-floor Observation Hall looks across the bay to Sakurajima.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 15 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east towards Kagoshima Aquarium. The building will be right in front of you.

card.hook: This museum is about 83 metres across, so your phone will give up on it unless you take a few steps back. Do it anyway, because the river next to it makes the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Museum of the Meiji Restoration, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the main frontage, then step back or sideways until the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close to the building, then switch to 1x once you've found room to step back. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then move in for the entrance or a sign.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime is easiest, because the even light shows the whole front clearly. Early morning is likely to be quieter, so fewer people will wander through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden Nanshu Bridge (南州橋) over the Kōtsuki River, the crossing visitors use on the way to the museum. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the bridge, or the stone lanterns just before it, fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and pose on the open ground in front of the reconstructed samurai houses, just in front of the museum, then ask them to step back so the whole museum fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules can differ between galleries inside, so check the signs at the door and ask staff if you're unsure.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a close-up of a sign or doorway, and see if a friend can guess it's the same building.
card.good_to_know: The museum (Ishin-furusato-kan) sits beside the Kōtsuki River in Kagoshima. The basement hall uses sound, light and robots to tell the story of the Meiji Restoration. The first floor covers the people, things and events of Satsuma Province. Entry may be ticketed and hours may vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Museum of the Meiji Restoration, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the main frontage, then step back or sideways until the whole building fits.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: Kagoshima Castle has no tower at all. It's a wide, calm site of moats and low walls, so your photo is all about the gateway and the setting.
card.stand_here: Start near 国道10号, at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m south-east of the subject. Face north-west towards the castle and take a few steps either side to dodge people or railings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate or wall as you see it. Go to 0.5x if you're close and want the gate and sky together, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof details and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gate, then slide to darker a touch if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework shows its texture.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. In the morning the sun is behind you as you face north-west, so the front of the site is nicely lit. Midday can look flat and harsh.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the foot of the Goromon Gate (Tsurumaru Castle Ruins) with the gate filling the background behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the gate in, and keep the castle over your shoulder. For a second backdrop, the footbridge over the moat has the surviving stone walls behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the castle grounds and the museums may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one wide to show the calm setting, one close on the stonework. Then see which one you'd actually send to your friends.
card.good_to_know: Shimazu Tadatsune built this as a large fortified residence, finished in 1604, with moats and low walls but no keep. Much of the original burned down in the 1870s. The Otemon main gate was rebuilt from surviving documents and photographs, finished in 2020, and the ruins became a National Historic Site in 2023.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near 国道10号, at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m south-east of the subject. Face north-west towards the castle and take a few steps either side to dodge people or railings.

card.hook: Most shrines have a famous gate. This one has a tree that looks like a bird mid-flap, wings spread wide, right on the path in. You'll spot it before you read a single sign.
card.stand_here: Stand at Terukuni Shrine on the approach, right at the pruned tree, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the tree so the worship hall is behind it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the tree with the hall behind it. Try 2x to pick out details of the tree or the hall without walking right up to them. Save 0.5x for the big white torii.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tree on one of the vertical lines and keep your phone fairly low, so those wings stand out against the building.
card.best_time: Early morning is quieter and the light is softer. Late afternoon gives you warmer, golden light.
card.selfie_here: The bird-shaped tree in the middle of the approach is a popular quick selfie spot. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and switch to 0.5x so the tree fits in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement next to the museum, facing the big white torii, while you stand in front of the gate. They should stay out of the road.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the grounds, but keep out of worshippers' way and don't photograph the inner hall. Never stand in the road under the torii, because traffic runs around it. Use the pavement.
card.challenge: Get the bird tree and the hall in one frame, then see if a friend can guess the shrine from the photo alone.
card.good_to_know: Terukuni Shrine was founded in 1882, in the Meiji period. It honours Shimazu Nariakira, whose posthumous name, Terukuni Daimyōjin, gives the shrine its name. It belongs to a very small group of shrines set up to honour people who were ordinary subjects of the Emperor in life.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Terukuni Shrine on the approach, right at the pruned tree, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the tree so the worship hall is behind it.

card.hook: A Ferris wheel on a shopping centre roof sounds like a joke, but Amuran is Kagoshima's party trick: a big, clean circle of sky sitting right on top of the city.
card.stand_here: Stand in Kagoshima-Chuo Station East Exit Station Square, on the east exit side of the station, and face Amu Plaza. Look up and you'll spot the wheel above the building.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the whole wheel from here. Go to 0.5x if you want the building and the street in too, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the gondolas.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the wheel's centre near a crossing point and keep the phone level so the building's edges stay straight.
card.best_time: Daytime with a clear sky shows the round shape most cleanly. Around dusk, when the sky turns deep blue, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little low and out to the side so the wheel peeks over your shoulder. Check the screen to make sure the whole circle made it in.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want to ride for a second shot from inside a gondola, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Be patient and wait for one bright gondola to drift into a nice spot on the rim, then tap the shutter button.
card.good_to_know: Amuran is 60 m across and reaches 91 m above the ground at its highest point. It has 36 gondolas, two of them fully transparent, and one full turn takes about 14 and a half minutes. It opened in September 2004 and had carried more than a million riders by May 2007.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Kagoshima-Chuo Station East Exit Station Square, on the east exit side of the station, and face Amu Plaza. Look up and you'll spot the wheel above the building.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Amuran behind the visitor, or a spot for a passer-by to shoot the visitor with the whole wheel in frame, so I have left both empty rather than guess. Named places I could find: Amu Square, the area connecting Kagoshima-Chūō Station and Amu Plaza, used for events (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amu_Plaza_Kagoshima). Amu Plaza Kagoshima's Wikipedia page says it sits north of the station's east gate, but no page says this square is a photo spot, so I have not listed it. One airial.travel page says the best way to photograph the wheel is from the ground, especially at night, but it names no ground location (https://www.airial.travel/attractions/japan/kagoshima/amuran-ferris-wheel-f_TN2Q-R). Sources also disagree on where the wheel is: Wikipedia says it sits on the roof of Amu Plaza, while Kupi and others say the 6th floor of the main building (https://www.kupi.com/en/explore/japan/kagoshima/amuran-ferris-wheel). The position you gave (31.58411, 130.54266) is close to the wheel's listed GPS of 31.58472, 130.54250 (https://aroundus.com/p/164490799-amuran). Rules: the only photography rule I found is general (personal photography is generally allowed, professional shoots may need permission), which is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, and the one tripod remark says only 'check if they are allowed'. No selfie-stick or tripod rule is stated, so none is listed. Safety: left blank because the only safety mention is about ride seatbelts, not photos. Suggestion: check on site at the Amu Plaza 6F ride entrance or the station plaza before relying on a spot.

card.hook: Here's a museum that doesn't live in a street, it lives inside an old castle's grounds, and that's the whole charm. The site is nearly 200 metres across, so your first job is simply fitting it all in.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the centre of the Reimeikan outline inside the Tsurumaru Castle grounds in Kagoshima. Then wander around the grounds until you find a clean angle that shows the museum with the castle surroundings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole big site into the frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for any details that catch your eye.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines to keep the walls level, and if the sky is bright, tap the museum and slide it a touch darker so it doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. If other visitors wander into your frame, just wait a moment for a clear view.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera and try zoom 0.5x so you get more of the scene behind you. Hold the phone a little higher, tilt it slightly down, and keep the museum and castle grounds over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for opening hours and admission before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot that shows how big the site is, then one close-up of the first detail that makes you stop. Bonus points if both are perfectly level!
card.good_to_know: Reimeikan is the Kagoshima prefectural museum of history and culture. It opened in 1983 and shows material about the history and culture of Kagoshima Prefecture. It stands in the grounds of Tsurumaru Castle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the centre of the Reimeikan outline inside the Tsurumaru Castle grounds in Kagoshima. Then wander around the grounds until you find a clean angle that shows the museum with the castle surroundings.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with Reimeikan directly behind them, so I have listed no selfie spots. The nearest documented photo area is the Goromon Gate, which stands in front of the castle residence that now houses Reimeikan. Sources describe photographing the gate, not the museum behind the visitor. Its outside area is free to enter, and one guide says it gets busy around midday on weekends and holidays. Photo-credit listings on Wikimedia Commons include titles such as 'View in front of Reimeikan' and 'Stele in front of Reimeikan', but those pages give no vantage point, so I did not use them. For a passer-by shot of the whole building, no page gives a position, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page I found states any selfie stick or tripod rule for this site. The Shiroyama Observatory pages warn about unlit dirt paths, but that is a different site, so I left the safety field blank.

card.hook: Picture four neat stone arches in front of you and a smoking volcano parked across the bay behind them. That's the deal at Ishibashi Park, and it's a pretty good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on the walkway near 西田橋 (Nishida-bashi), a short distance from the bridge. Face the water and Sakurajima, so the four-arch stone bridge sits in front of you and the volcano rises across Kinko Bay behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits all four arches and Sakurajima in one frame. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to make the volcano look bigger behind the bridge. Save 0.5x for the wooden gate, or for the full length of a bridge when you're up close.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the water line level, then tap the sky or the volcano and drag the slider a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when one guide says the light falls on the bridge from the front. Pick a clear day, because Sakurajima can vanish in cloud or haze. If haze is hiding it, try 2x to 5x rather than going wider.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie right on Nishida-bashi, where the Nishidabashi Gomon Gate comes into view after you cross. It's a good spot for commemorative photos. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene, and check what's behind you before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the path leaving the park's parking lot, where Nishida Bridge is on your right as you walk, to take a photo of you with the bridge in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photography for personal use is generally fine in the park, but respect other visitors and any signs in the park or museum. Sakurajima is an active volcano, so check local volcano activity updates before you head over.
card.challenge: Get the arches, the volcano and the water all in one frame, with the water filling the bottom of the picture, and see if you can do it without a single stranger's head in it.
card.good_to_know: The park keeps three of the old Edo-period stone bridges that once carried roads over the Kōtsuki River. Two of the original five collapsed in the floods of August 1993, and the survivors were moved here, restored, and opened as a park in 2000. 西田橋 was used by daimyō lords on their trips to and from Edo, which is why so much was spent on it. Look for the statue of Iwanaga Sangorō, the mason who built all five bridges.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the walkway near 西田橋 (Nishida-bashi), a short distance from the bridge. Face the water and Sakurajima, so the four-arch stone bridge sits in front of you and the volcano rises across Kinko Bay behind it.

card.hook: Picture a tidy white wooden house with open verandahs, sitting calmly behind a quiet front yard. It's all that's left of a whole cotton mill, and it's a very easy building to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in the front yard (前庭) facing the facade, so the two-storey house with its open verandahs fills the view. The old mill site is to the south-west of where you're standing.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole front. If both floors and the verandahs won't fit, switch to 0.5x and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the verandah posts with the vertical lines so the house stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the light is even and the white walls look clean. An overcast sky works well for a building this pale.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the porch of the white residence with the building behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in the arched verandas, and hold the phone a little low so the house rises up behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Interior photography isn't allowed, so keep all your photos outside. Check the official site for visiting arrangements before you go. Traffic nearby is heavy, so take care if you step back toward the road for a wider shot.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the whole house, then one close-up where the repeated posts and railings make a pattern. Two photos, two moods.
card.good_to_know: The house was finished in 1867 for the British engineers who came to set up Satsuma's cotton mill, and they went home after only a year. It later served as a cannon-factory office and, in 1877, as a temporary hospital during the Satsuma Rebellion. It was moved to Kagoshima Castle in 1884, returned to its original spot in 1936, and the mill site is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing from 2015.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in the front yard (前庭) facing the facade, so the two-storey house with its open verandahs fills the view. The old mill site is to the south-west of where you're standing.

selfie_spots.why: Sources single out the porch and arched verandas as the building's signature features, so it makes a natural backdrop for a selfie.
